readerTitle: Why the better tape lost: open vs closed
caseNote: 실제 기업 (JVC·Sony의 VHS 대 Betamax, IBM PC) + 가상 적용 (주택 수리 회사의 예약 앱)
insight: 개방이냐 폐쇄냐는 시장을 얼마나 키울지와 그 시장에서 내 몫을 얼마나 지킬지 사이의 선택이며, 전부 열거나 전부 닫는 대신 층마다 다르게 정할 수 있다.
misconception: 더 좋은 제품을 만들어 혼자 쥐고 있으면 이긴다. 또는 반대로, 무조건 열면 이긴다.

sources.text: Cusumano, M., Mylonadis, Y., & Rosenbloom, R. (1992). Strategic Maneuvering and Mass-Market Dynamics: The Triumph of VHS over Beta. Business History Review.
IBM, company history: the IBM Personal Computer (1981) and sale of the PC business to Lenovo (2005)

factChecks.note: Betamax 출시 1975년, VHS 출시 1976년(일본). 초기 녹화 시간 Betamax 약 1시간, VHS 약 2시간이라는 통설을 게시 전 확인하세요. 카드에는 'about one hour', 'about two hours'로 적었습니다.
JVC가 마쓰시타(파나소닉)를 포함한 더 많은 제조사에 VHS를 라이선스했고, Sony도 일부 제조사(Toshiba, Sanyo 등)에 Beta를 공유했지만 진영이 더 작았다는 점을 확인하세요. 카드에는 'a smaller group of partners'로 표현했습니다.
Sony가 1988년에 VHS 녹화기 판매를 시작했다는 사실을 확인하세요.
VHS 승리의 원인(녹화 시간, 비디오 대여점의 재고 선택, 라이선스 전략)은 연구자마다 비중을 다르게 봅니다. 카드에 'historians still debate'로 적었습니다.
IBM PC(1981)가 외부 부품(Intel 프로세서, Microsoft 운영체제)을 쓰고 기술 문서를 공개했으며, Compaq 등 호환 기종이 시장을 넓혔고, IBM이 2005년 PC 사업을 Lenovo에 매각했다는 내용을 확인하세요. 구체적 점유율 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why the better tape lost: open vs closed
body: In 1975, Sony launched Betamax, a home video recorder many engineers admired. A year later, JVC launched a rival format: VHS.
Within about a decade, VHS ruled living rooms worldwide. In 1988, Sony itself started selling VHS machines. Picture quality was not the deciding factor.

image.label: Two video cassettes, one small and alone, one surrounded by many hands
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 작은 카세트 하나가 홀로 서 있고, 오른쪽 카세트는 여러 공장·상점 모양의 작은 손들이 함께 들어 올리고 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You've invented a new video format.
body: It's the mid-1970s. Your format works well, and a rival format is coming. Other electronics makers would like to build machines using your design.
What do you do?

options.text: Keep it to yourself so every machine sold is yours
options.feedback: You keep all the profit per machine and full control of quality. But you must build the whole market alone, at your own speed.

options.text: License it widely to other makers for a fee
options.feedback: More factories, more shops and more brands push your format at once. You earn less per machine and lose some control.

options.text: Share it with a few hand-picked partners
options.feedback: A middle path: some extra reach, most of the control. It works only if those few partners are enough to win.

choice.afterReveal: JVC leaned toward B and recruited a large group of makers. Sony shared Betamax with a smaller group of partners. Next card: what happened.

cards.title: More makers meant more machines, then more tapes.
body: JVC brought in a big group of manufacturers, including Matsushita, one of Japan's largest electronics firms. Sony's Betamax camp stayed smaller.
More makers meant more VHS machines in shops at more price points. Video rental stores then stocked more VHS tapes, which made buying a VHS machine even safer.
Historians still debate the full cause. VHS also recorded about two hours at launch, versus about one hour for Betamax. But wide licensing helped VHS **snowball**.

cards.title: Open vs closed
body: An **open** business lets others build, sell, connect to or copy parts of what you make. A **closed** business keeps those parts to itself.
Open tends to grow the market faster, because many partners push at once. Closed tends to keep more profit and control per sale, because you own the whole experience.
The real question is not which is better. It's which one you need more right now: **a bigger market or a bigger share of it**.

image.label: A dial between 'Open' and 'Closed'
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데 큰 다이얼, 왼쪽 끝 'Closed: more control, more profit per sale', 오른쪽 끝 'Open: more partners, faster growth'. 다이얼 바늘은 중간쯤을 가리킴.

cards.softwareNote: In software, openness often means public APIs, plug-ins or open-source code. Letting outside developers connect to your product can multiply what it does, but they may also build the features you hoped to sell.

cards.title: What each side buys you.
body: Each choice gives you something and costs you something.
list: **Open gains:** speed, reach, more partners and complements, a better chance to become the standard
**Open costs:** less profit per sale, less control over quality, rivals can use what you shared
**Closed gains:** higher margins, a consistent experience, decisions stay yours
**Closed costs:** slower growth, and you carry every investment alone
cards.callout: Open tends to win a race to become the standard. Closed tends to win when the experience itself is what customers pay for.

cards.title: It's a dial, not a switch.
body: Few businesses are fully open or fully closed. Most open some layers and close others.

A franchise shares its recipes and brand with owners, but keeps the supply chain and the rules. A kitchen-appliance maker might publish its fitting sizes so any cabinet maker can build around it, while keeping the motor design secret.
The skill is choosing **which layer to open**: usually the one where partners add value, not the one where your profit lives.

cards.title: Open can grow a market you don't own.
body: In 1981, IBM built its personal computer from outside parts, including an Intel processor and a Microsoft operating system, and published its technical details. The design spread fast and became the standard.
But others could build the same machine. Clone makers such as Compaq sold compatible PCs, and much of the profit flowed to the parts suppliers. In 2005, IBM sold its PC business to Lenovo.
Openness is also hard to undo. Once partners rely on what you shared, taking it back costs trust.

cards.title: Now it's a home-repair company.
body: Your plumbing company built a booking app homeowners love. Independent electricians, painters and cleaners ask to offer their services through it.
What do you do?

options.text: Keep it closed: only your own plumbers in the app
options.feedback: You protect quality and your margins. But homeowners may switch to an app that covers every job in the house.

options.text: Open it to anyone who signs up
options.feedback: The app fills up fast. But one bad painter damages trust in your name, and you have no say in who shows up at the door.

options.text: Open it to vetted partners who follow your quality rules, and take a booking fee
options.feedback: You gain reach and a new revenue stream, while keeping the layer that matters most: the customer's trust. It takes work to vet and police partners.

cards.title: Open to grow the pie. Close to keep your slice.
body: Decide layer by layer what others may build on, and keep closed the part where your profit and trust live.
**Try it today:** list three things partners or rivals could use from your business: a method, a tool, a customer list. Mark each one open, closed or open with rules, and write one reason for each.
